summary.heading: Charged particles in a uniform electric field
summary.html:
• In a uniform field a charge feels a constant force $F = qE$ (along $E$ for a positive charge, opposite for a negative one), so a constant acceleration $a = \dfrac{qE}{m}$: the A.1 equations of motion apply.
  • Accelerated from rest through a p.d. $V$:
$$\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = qV$$
  • Entering the field at right angles: constant velocity along the plates, constant acceleration across them, so the path is a parabola (like a horizontally thrown ball). After leaving the field it moves in a straight line.
  • An electric field can change a particle's speed (it does work on it).

summary.heading: The magnetic force on a moving charge
summary.html:
$$F = qvB\sin\theta$$
  • $\theta$ is the angle between the velocity and the field. Greatest when $v \perp B$; zero when parallel. A stationary charge feels no magnetic force.
  • Direction: perpendicular to both $v$ and $B$. Fleming's left-hand rule: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current (direction a positive charge moves), thuMb = force. For a negative charge, reverse the force.
  • The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work: speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only the direction changes.

summary.heading: Circular motion and the charge-to-mass ratio
summary.html:
• Moving at right angles to a uniform $B$, the force provides the centripetal force: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so
$$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$
  • Faster or heavier particles make bigger circles; a stronger field or bigger charge, smaller ones. Opposite charges curve opposite ways.
  • Period $T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$: independent of speed.
  • A velocity component along the field is unaffected, so the particle spirals in a helix along the field lines (the aurora).
  • Charge-to-mass ratio: $\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{v}{Br}$. In the school experiment (electrons accelerated through $V$, bent into a circle by coils), combining $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV$ with $v = \dfrac{eBr}{m}$ gives $\dfrac{e}{m} = \dfrac{2V}{B^2r^2}$.
  • A mass spectrometer uses the same idea: ions with the same charge and speed curve by amounts that depend on their mass, so isotopes separate.

summary.heading: Crossed electric and magnetic fields
summary.html:
• With $E$, $B$ and $v$ all mutually perpendicular, the electric and magnetic forces can be opposite. When they balance, the particle goes straight through:
$$qE = qvB \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \frac{E}{B}$$
  • This velocity selector passes one speed only, whatever the charge or mass. Slower particles are deflected in the direction of the electric force; faster ones in the direction of the magnetic force.

summary.heading: Forces on current-carrying wires
summary.html:
$$F = BIL\sin\theta$$
  • The motor effect: $\theta$ is between the wire and the field; no force when parallel. Direction from Fleming's left-hand rule (second finger along the current). It follows from $F = qvB\sin\theta$ because $qv = IL$.
  • Field round a long straight wire: concentric circles (right-hand grip rule). New for 2028 its size is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$: proportional to $I$, inversely proportional to $r$. $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{T m A}^{-1}$.
$$\frac{F}{L} = \mu_0\frac{I_1I_2}{2\pi r}$$
  • Each wire sits in the other's field. Currents in the same direction attract; opposite directions repel.
  • The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite (Newton's third law), even if the currents differ.
  • The old definition of the ampere used this force: $2 \times 10^{-7}$ N per metre for 1 A in wires 1 m apart.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Saying a magnetic field speeds a charge up: it changes only the direction (an electric field can change the speed).
  • Forgetting to reverse Fleming's rule for negative charges such as electrons.
  • Using the wrong angle in $\sin\theta$: it is between the velocity (or current) and the field.
  • Mixing up the paths: uniform $E$ gives a parabola; perpendicular uniform $B$ gives a circle.
  • Saying the wire with the bigger current feels the bigger force.
  • Getting attraction and repulsion of parallel wires the wrong way round (same direction attracts).
  • Forgetting to convert mT to T and cm to m.

Experiments: Thomson found a charge-to-mass ratio over 1000 times that of hydrogen ions (the modern value is about 1840). Why did that suggest a new, tiny particle rather than an unusually highly charged atom?
Show a fine-beam tube (or a video of one). What would have to be measured to repeat Thomson's reasoning in the lab?
Models: Field lines plus $F = qvB\sin\theta$ let us predict a particle's path exactly. Does the model need the field to be 'real' to work?
Where does the simple circular-path model fail (particles near light speed, non-uniform fields, particles losing energy in a bubble chamber)?
Measurement: Until 2019 the ampere was defined by the force between wires; now it is defined by fixing $e$. Why might a definition based on a constant of nature be better?
Discuss: if we fix the value of $e$ by definition, can we still measure it?
Global impact: List places where steering charged particles matters: hospitals, airports, forensics, space missions. Which surprised students most?
Who should pay for huge accelerators whose benefits are uncertain when they are built?

oracy.html:
Think–pair–share (1 minute alone, 3 minutes in pairs, then pairs report to the class). Claim: "A strong enough magnetic field can be used to speed up a beam of protons, just as an electric field can."

  • We think … because …
  • The direction of the force is …
  • The strongest objection to our view is …

Listen for: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work: it changes the direction, not the speed; only the electric field can change the protons' kinetic energy.

Is a field pattern like a map?: A map leaves out most of the landscape to be useful. What does a field-line diagram leave out?
Can a map ever be 'wrong' if it is useful for its purpose? Can a field diagram?
How do we know about particles we can't: List the chain of inferences from a bent beam to 'there is an electron'. Which step needs the most trust?
Is indirect evidence weaker than seeing something? Is seeing through a microscope 'direct'?
Why so many hand rules?: Have students try Fleming's left-hand rule and a right-hand slap rule on the same problem. Do they always agree?
If the physics is the same, why do different countries keep different conventions? What is lost by changing?
Who owns discoveries made with huge mach: The Higgs boson papers had thousands of authors. Who deserves the credit, and how should prizes deal with that?
If no one person understands the whole experiment, how do they know it is right?

videos.title: e/m Apparatus with New Tube
videos.use: Shows the electron beam bent into a circle in a fine-beam tube. Use it if the school has no tube, then have students take readings from the screen and calculate $e/m$.

videos.title: The Interaction Bewtween an Electron Beam and a Magnetic Field
videos.use: A short demonstration of an electron beam deflected by a magnet. Pause and ask students to predict the direction with Fleming's left-hand rule (remembering the electrons are negative).

videos.title: How Special Relativity Makes Magnets Work
videos.use: Extension after the force between parallel wires: why a current-carrying wire pushes on a moving charge, explained with relativity. For keen students; not examined.
